newsitem.title: USA: Clinton condemns killing of seven Israeli girls.
newsitem.headline: Clinton condemns killing of seven Israeli girls.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday condemned the shooting of seven Israeli girls by a Jordanian soldier as "inexcusable and tragic" but said there was no evidence the killings were politically motivated and appealed for calm in the region.

"Today along the normally peaceful border between Israel and Jordan we have seen an inexcusable and tragic act of violence against schoolchildren. I condemn this act in the strongest possible terms," Clinton said.
"There is no evidence at this moment that this terrible incident is related to the tensions in the area over the issues," he said as he left the White House for a visit to North Carolina.
"For all we know this may have been just a deranged person," he said. "We have no reason to believe this was politically motivated by any larger group or anything. We just don't know that."

A Jordanian soldier on Thursday shot and killed seven Israeli schoolgirls who were on a fieldtrip to an Israeli-Jordanian border site called "The Island of Peace." The soldier trained his rifle on the girls, aged 12 to 14, as they walked to an observation point overlooking Syria and the Golan Heights.
Israeli officials said the man, who was overpowered by other soldiers, appeared to be acting alone.

A White House spokeswoman said Clinton spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from Air Force One for 10 minutes to convey his condolences over the killings, which occurred amid growing tensions in the region.

A series of events including Israeli decisions to build new housing for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem and to hand over less West Bank territory than the Palestinians had expected have badly strained relations in the region.

Earlier this week the king sent Netanyahu an anguished letter suggesting he had lost trust in the Israeli prime minister and warning him of the potential for violence. "I could remain aloof if the very lives of all Arabs and Israelis and their future were not fast sliding towards an abyss of bloodshed, brought about by fear and despair," he said in the letter.

Hussein had been scheduled to meet Clinton in Washington on Tuesday, the fourth in a series of visits here by Middle East leaders seeking to revive the peace process, but a Jordanian official told Israel radio he would delay the visit.
White House officials said they had not been officially informed of whether Hussein still planned to make the visit.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israel's Netanyahu have all travelled to Washington to meet Clinton in the past month.

Clinton said no one should jump to any conclusions about the shooting "given King Hussein and Jordan's long record of reaching for peace and reconciliation," and he urged leaders in the region to redouble their efforts for peace.

"The leaders in the region must work hard to calm the situation, to do everything in their power to create an atmosphere in which violence is rejected rather than embraced. We call on the leaders ... to reject violence, to redouble their efforts toward peace and reconciliation," he said.
Defence Secretary William Cohen, travelling with Clinton to North Carolina, suggested that the killings might generate further resistance to the peace process within Israel.

"When something like this occurs it's going to create even more opposition within the state of Israel in terms of moving forward," Cohen said, adding: "I think it'll be a temporary setback but we will proceed along the path of peace."
